questions.sec: Supranuclear control of ocular movements and vestibular tests
questions.q: The FEF and PEF of the frontal cortex in the book initiate which ocular movements?
questions.exp: Frontal cortex: FEF (frontal eye field), PEF (parietal eye field) — initiates saccades: rapid, fixating movements. (Book p59)

questions.sec: Supranuclear control of ocular movements and vestibular tests
questions.q: Match the cortical centre with its control of gaze in the book — 1) Frontal cortex (FEF/PEF) 2) Occipital cortex … A) Initiates pursuits, slow following movements — controlled ipsilaterally B) Initiates saccades — horizontal controlled contralaterally, vertical controlled bilaterally
questions.exp: Frontal cortex: saccades; horizontal controlled C/L, vertical B/L. Occipital cortex: initiates pursuits (slow following movements), controlled I/L. (Book p59)

questions.sec: Supranuclear control of ocular movements and vestibular tests
questions.q: Fill up: the vestibular apparatus in the book is located in the ______, maintaining movement of the head along with the eye.
questions.exp: Vestibular apparatus: in the ear, to maintain movement of head along with the eye. (Book p59)

questions.sec: Supranuclear control of ocular movements and vestibular tests
questions.q: Fill up: the vestibular apparatus gives rise to the VOR and the ______ reflex.
questions.exp: Vestibular apparatus → VOR (vestibulo ocular reflex) and optokinetic reflex. (Book p59)

questions.sec: Supranuclear control of ocular movements and vestibular tests
questions.q: The oculo-cephalic reflex in the book is AKA:
questions.exp: Oculo-cephalic reflex: AKA Doll's reflex — tests CN III, VI, VIII; eyes move opposite to the movement of head (in coma patients). (Book p59)

questions.sec: Supranuclear control of ocular movements and vestibular tests
questions.q: Match the vestibular test with its finding in the book — 1) Oculo-cephalic (Doll's) reflex 2) Caloric test — cold water 3) Caloric test — warm water … A) Opposite side nystagmus B) Tests CN III, VI, VIII — eyes move opposite to head movement (in coma patients) C) Same side nystagmus
questions.exp: Doll's reflex tests CN III, VI, VIII with eyes moving opposite to head movement in coma; caloric test (injection of water into ear): cold water → opposite side nystagmus; warm water → same side nystagmus. (Book p59)

questions.sec: Supranuclear control of ocular movements and vestibular tests
questions.q: In a comatose patient, rapidly rotating the head makes the eyes dart opposite to the head movement. Per the book this Doll's reflex is used to test:
questions.exp: Oculo-cephalic (Doll's) reflex: test CN III, VI, VIII; eyes move opposite to the movement of head (in coma patients). (Book p59)

questions.sec: Supranuclear control of ocular movements and vestibular tests
questions.q: Which statement about the caloric test is FALSE per the book?
opts: It involves injection of water into the ear
Cold water produces opposite side nystagmus
Warm water produces same side nystagmus
Cold water produces same side nystagmus
questions.exp: Caloric test: cold water → opposite side nystagmus; warm water → same side nystagmus. (Book p59)

questions.sec: The horizontal gaze pathway
questions.q: Fill up: the centre for horizontal gaze in the book is the ______ PPRF.
questions.exp: Horizontal gaze: centre — ipsilateral PPRF; saccadic movements to look towards the left/right side. (Book p60)

questions.sec: The horizontal gaze pathway
questions.q: Fill up: in the book's pathway of left gaze, PPRF stands for ______.
questions.exp: PPRF: paraporentine (paramedian pontine) reticular formation; MLF: medial longitudinal fasciculus. (Book p60)

questions.sec: The horizontal gaze pathway
questions.q: Match the station in the book's pathway of left gaze with its role — 1) C/L FEF (right) 2) I/L PPRF (left) 3) I/L 6th nerve nucleus 4) C/L MLF → C/L 3rd nerve nucleus … A) Centre — drives the left LR B) Initiates the gaze C) Drives the left lateral rectus D) Drives the right MR (yoke muscle)
questions.exp: Pathway of left gaze: initiation — C/L FEF; centre — I/L PPRF; I/L 6th nucleus → left LR; C/L MLF → C/L 3rd nucleus → right MR. (Book p60)

questions.sec: The horizontal gaze pathway
questions.q: In the book's left gaze circuit, the signal that crosses the midline to activate the contralateral 3rd nerve nucleus travels through the:
questions.exp: The C/L MLF carries the gaze signal to the C/L 3rd nerve nucleus, which drives the yoke (right MR). (Book p60)

questions.sec: The horizontal gaze pathway
questions.q: Horizontal gaze per the book produces:
opts: Pursuit movements following a moving target
Saccadic movements to look towards the left/right side
Convergence movements towards a near object
questions.exp: Horizontal gaze: saccadic movements to look towards left/right side. (Book p60)

questions.sec: The horizontal gaze pathway
questions.q: Fill up: in the book's left gaze diagram, MLF stands for ______.
questions.exp: MLF: medial longitudinal fasciculus. (Book p60)

questions.sec: The horizontal gaze pathway
questions.q: Which statement about the horizontal gaze circuit is FALSE per the book?
opts: The centre is the ipsilateral PPRF
Initiation comes from the contralateral FEF
The 6th nucleus drives the ipsilateral lateral rectus
The 6th nucleus drives the contralateral lateral rectus
questions.exp: The 6th nerve nucleus innervates the IPSILATERAL lateral rectus; the contralateral MR is driven via the C/L MLF to the 3rd nucleus. (Book p60)

questions.sec: Horizontal gaze palsy and the one-and-a-half syndrome
questions.q: In the book's horizontal gaze palsy table, the lesion that produces internuclear ophthalmoplegia is at the:
questions.exp: C/L MLF lesion: internuclear ophthalmoplegia — m/c cause multiple sclerosis. (Book p61)

questions.sec: Horizontal gaze palsy and the one-and-a-half syndrome
questions.q: The m/c cause of internuclear ophthalmoplegia per the book is:
questions.exp: C/L MLF: internuclear ophthalmoplegia; m/c cause: multiple sclerosis. (Book p61)

questions.sec: Horizontal gaze palsy and the one-and-a-half syndrome
questions.q: Fill up: in the C/L MLF row of the book's table, the I/L LR ______ contract while the C/L MR fails to contract.
questions.exp: C/L MLF (INO): I/L LR can contract (abduction present); C/L MR fails to contract (adduction absent) → left gaze defect: I/L adduction absent, C/L abduction present. (Book p61)

questions.sec: Horizontal gaze palsy and the one-and-a-half syndrome
questions.q: A 32-year-old with multiple sclerosis shows a left gaze defect: the left eye fails to adduct, but the right eye abducts normally. Per the book this pattern is:
questions.exp: INO: I/L adduction absent, C/L abduction present — the book's left gaze defect of the C/L MLF row. (Book p61)

questions.sec: Horizontal gaze palsy and the one-and-a-half syndrome
questions.q: A lesion of the C/L FEF or the I/L PPRF in the book's table produces:
opts: Bitemporal hemianopia with a chiasmal lesion
INO with I/L adduction absent and C/L abduction present
A head tilt with chin down and facial turn
Left gaze palsy — I/L LR and C/L MR both fail to contract
questions.exp: C/L FEF or I/L PPRF lesion: I/L LR fails to contract and C/L MR fails to contract → left gaze palsy. (Book p61)

questions.sec: Horizontal gaze palsy and the one-and-a-half syndrome
questions.q: The book's combined I/L MLF + I/L PPRF lesion pattern is named the ______ syndrome.
questions.exp: One and a half syndrome: I/L MLF → C/L gaze defect + I/L PPRF → I/L gaze palsy = 1½ defect. (Book p61)

questions.sec: Horizontal gaze palsy and the one-and-a-half syndrome
questions.q: Fill up: in the book's one-and-a-half figure, right gaze (defect) from a left MLF lesion shows ______ loss of left gaze, while left gaze (palsy) from a left PPRF lesion shows ______ loss of left gaze.
questions.exp: Figure: primary gaze normal; right gaze (defect) due to lesion of left MLF — partial loss of left gaze; left gaze (palsy) due to lesion of left PPRF — completely loss of left gaze. (Book p61)

questions.sec: Horizontal gaze palsy and the one-and-a-half syndrome
questions.q: Which statement about the horizontal gaze palsy table is FALSE?
opts: A C/L FEF lesion → left gaze palsy in the table
An I/L PPRF lesion → left gaze palsy in the table
In the C/L MLF row, I/L LR fails while C/L MR can contract
INO is the m/c problem due to multiple sclerosis
questions.exp: In the C/L MLF (INO) row the I/L LR CAN contract and the C/L MR fails to contract — the reverse of the false option. (Book p61)

questions.sec: Vertical gaze pathway and etiologies of vertical gaze palsy
questions.q: The 1° centre of the vertical gaze pathway in the book is the:
questions.exp: Vertical gaze pathway: 1° centre — rimLF; 2° centre — INC. (Book p62)

questions.sec: Vertical gaze pathway and etiologies of vertical gaze palsy
questions.q: The 2° centre of the vertical gaze pathway in the book is the:
questions.exp: 2° centre — INC (interstitial nucleus of Cajal). (Book p62)

questions.sec: Vertical gaze pathway and etiologies of vertical gaze palsy
questions.q: Fill up: in the book, rimLF stands for ______.
questions.exp: rimLF: rostral interstitial medial longitudinal fasciculus; INC: interstitial nucleus of Cajal. (Book p62)

questions.sec: Vertical gaze pathway and etiologies of vertical gaze palsy
questions.q: Match the vertical gaze structure with its labelled role in the book's diagram — 1) Frontal and occipital centres 2) rimLF 3) INC … A) Cortical input to the pathway B) 1° centre C) 2° centre
questions.exp: Diagram: frontal and occipital centres (input) → rimLF (1° centre) and INC (2° centre), with superior colliculus and posterior commissure relaying to the trochlear and oculomotor nerve nuclei. (Book p62)

questions.sec: Vertical gaze pathway and etiologies of vertical gaze palsy
questions.q: The m/c etiology of vertical gaze palsy per the book is:
questions.exp: Etiology of vertical gaze palsy: 1. distal basilar artery ischaemia (m/c) — supplies rimLF. (Book p62)

questions.sec: Vertical gaze pathway and etiologies of vertical gaze palsy
questions.q: An 80-year-old man gradually loses downgaze, then upgaze, then all ocular movements, and finally convergence. Per the book the diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Progressive supranuclear palsy: palsy — downgaze → upgaze → global → convergence; occurs in old age. (Book p62)

questions.sec: Vertical gaze pathway and etiologies of vertical gaze palsy
questions.q: Match the Parinaud syndrome feature with its description in the book — 1) Collier's sign 2) Convergence 3) Light-near dissociation … A) Upper eyelid retraction B) Light reflex absent and near reflex present C) Retraction nystagmus
questions.exp: Parinaud clinical features: upgaze palsy (supranuclear); Collier's sign — upper eyelid retraction; convergence — retraction nystagmus; light-near dissociation — light reflex absent and near reflex present. (Book p62)

questions.sec: Vertical gaze pathway and etiologies of vertical gaze palsy
questions.q: Parinaud's dorsal midbrain syndrome per the book: the site of lesion is the ______, and the m/c cause is ______.
questions.exp: Parinaud's dorsal midbrain syndrome: site of lesion — posterior commissure; most common cause — pinealoma > hydrocephalus. (Book p62)

questions.sec: Vertical gaze pathway and etiologies of vertical gaze palsy
questions.q: Which statement about vertical gaze palsy is FALSE per the book?
opts: Collier's sign is upper eyelid retraction
Progressive supranuclear palsy occurs in old age
Light-near dissociation: light reflex present and near reflex absent
questions.exp: Light-near dissociation is the opposite: light reflex ABSENT and near reflex PRESENT. (Book p62)

questions.sec: Vertical gaze pathway and etiologies of vertical gaze palsy
questions.q: All of the following are listed in the book as structures of the vertical gaze pathway diagram EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Diagram structures: frontal and occipital centres, superior colliculus, rimLF, INC, posterior commissure, trochlear nerve nucleus, oculomotor nerve nucleus. (Book p62)

units.title: Supranuclear control of ocular movements and vestibular tests
units.guide: Cerebral cortex: frontal cortex (FEF — frontal eye field, PEF — parietal eye field) initiates saccades (rapid, fixating movements) — horizontal controlled contralaterally, vertical bilaterally; occipital cortex initiates pursuits (slow following movements), controlled ipsilaterally. Both feed the brainstem cranial nerve nuclei. Vestibular apparatus (in the ear) maintains movement of head along with the eye → VOR (vestibulo ocular reflex) and optokinetic reflex. Tests: oculo-cephalic reflex (AKA Doll's reflex) — tests CN III, VI, VIII; eyes move opposite to the movement of head (in coma patients). Caloric test (injection of water into ear): cold water → opposite side nystagmus; warm water → same side nystagmus.

units.title: The horizontal gaze pathway
units.guide: Horizontal gaze: centre — ipsilateral PPRF; saccadic movements to look towards the left/right side. Pathway of left gaze: initiation — C/L FEF (right) → I/L PPRF (left, centre) → I/L 6th nerve nucleus (drives the left LR) and via the C/L MLF → C/L 3rd nerve nucleus (drives the right MR yoke). PPRF: paraporentine/paramedian pontine reticular formation; MLF: medial longitudinal fasciculus.

units.title: Horizontal gaze palsy and the one-and-a-half syndrome
units.guide: Table: C/L FEF — I/L LR fails to contract, C/L MR fails to contract → left gaze palsy; I/L PPRF — same → left gaze palsy; C/L MLF — internuclear ophthalmoplegia (m/c cause multiple sclerosis): I/L LR can contract, C/L MR fails to contract → left gaze defect: I/L adduction absent, C/L abduction present. One and a half syndrome: I/L MLF → C/L gaze defect + I/L PPRF → I/L gaze palsy = 1½ defect; figure: primary gaze normal; right gaze (defect) d/t left MLF — partial loss of left gaze; left gaze (palsy) d/t left PPRF — completely loss of left gaze.

units.title: Vertical gaze pathway and etiologies of vertical gaze palsy
units.guide: Vertical gaze (upgaze/downgaze) pathway: frontal and occipital centres → superior colliculus, rimLF, INC, posterior commissure → trochlear and oculomotor nerve nuclei. 1° centre — rimLF (rostral interstitial medial longitudinal fasciculus); 2° centre — INC (interstitial nucleus of Cajal). Etiology of vertical gaze palsy: 1. distal basilar artery ischaemia (m/c) — supplies rimLF; a. progressive supranuclear palsy — palsy: downgaze → upgaze → global → convergence, occurs in old age; 3. Parinaud's dorsal midbrain syndrome — site: posterior commissure; m/c cause: pinealoma > hydrocephalus; features: upgaze palsy (supranuclear), Collier's sign (upper eyelid retraction), convergence — retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation (light reflex absent and near reflex present).
